angles: Trigger.dev vs serverless platforms: unlike AWS Lambda and Vercel which have hard timeouts, Trigger.dev tasks have absolutely no timeouts — critical for long-running AI agent conversations that may span hours or days

Durable sub-agents as a differentiator: Trigger.dev's sub-agent pattern (AgentChat) lets you delegate work to independent durable agents that stream results back — this is architecturally different from simple function calls or tool invocations

HITL as a first-class primitive: Trigger.dev's waitpoint tokens let agents pause mid-execution with full state checkpointed, consume zero compute while waiting, and resume with sub-second latency — not bolted on as an afterthought

The session-as-agent paradigm: Trigger.dev's chat.agent treats each conversation as a durable session that survives page refreshes, deploys, and crashes — this is the architectural shift from stateless request-response to stateful agent sessions

TypeScript-first agent development: Trigger.dev's Zod schema-based type safety means agent tools and inputs are validated at compile time, reducing runtime failures common in dynamically-typed agent frameworks
Production observability built in: every turn is a span in the Trigger.dev dashboard, sessions are queryable via sessions.list for inbox-style UIs — no separate observability stack needed
Comparison with alternatives: Trigger.dev vs Temporal (more developer-friendly, TypeScript-native), vs Inngest (deeper AI agent primitives), vs plain Claude Code (managed runtime with durability)

When to use Trigger.dev for AI agents: best for production TypeScript/Node.js applications needing durable execution, HITL approvals, and sub-agent orchestration — overkill for simple stateless chat completions
